title: Global Prevalence of Myopia and High Myopia and Temporal Trends from 2000 through 2050
authors: Holden BA, Fricke TR, Wilson DA, Jong M, Naidoo KS, Sankaridurg P, Wong TY, Naduvilath TJ, Resnikoff S
key_findings: Systematic review/meta-analysis: 145 studies covering 2.1 million participants, combined with UN Population Department and urbanisation data.
2000: 1406 million people with myopia (22.9%; 95% CI 932-1932 million) and 163 million with high myopia (2.7%).
2050 prediction: 4758 million with myopia (49.8%; 3620-6056 million) and 938 million with high myopia (9.8%; 479-2104 million).
Definitions used: myopia -0.50 D or less; high myopia -5.00 D or less (not the IMI -6.00 D cut-off).
practical_applications: Allowed wording: 'นักวิจัยคาดการณ์ว่าปี 2050 ประชากรโลกราวครึ่งหนึ่งอาจสายตาสั้น' — always say 'คาดการณ์', not 'จะเป็น'.
limitations: Projection from regression trends; wide uncertainty intervals.
Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 26875007); full text not read.
High myopia defined at -5.00 D, so the 9.8% is not directly comparable with IMI-defined high myopia.

title: Blindness and vision impairment (fact sheet)
key_findings: At least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment; at least 1 billion cases could have been prevented or are unaddressed.
Presbyopia is the main cause of near vision impairment, affecting 826 million people (unaddressed).
Unaddressed: cataract 94 million and uncorrected refractive error 88.4 million cases of distance impairment/blindness.
practical_applications: Use '826 ล้านคนทั่วโลกมีปัญหามองใกล้ไม่ชัดจากสายตายาวตามวัยที่ยังไม่ได้แก้ไข' — not '826 million have presbyopia' (total presbyopia is larger; secondary coverage of the WHO 2019 World report on vision cites ~1.8 billion, not verified here).
limitations: Fact sheet dated 10 Feb 2026; global, no Thai breakdown.
license: WHO terms (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for most WHO content)

title: IMI - Defining and Classifying Myopia: A Proposed Set of Standards for Clinical and Epidemiologic Studies
key_findings: Myopia: spherical equivalent refractive error ≤ −0.50 D when ocular accommodation is relaxed; low myopia ≤ −0.50 and > −6.00 D; high myopia ≤ −6.00 D.
Pre-myopia: ≤ +0.75 D and > −0.50 D in children whose baseline refraction, age and other risk factors make future myopia likely enough to merit prevention.

'There is no clear biological basis in terms of axial length, refraction or other ocular biometric parameter to differentiate high from lower degrees of myopia'; pathologic myopia is defined by structural changes.
practical_applications: Use standard definitions when a script says 'สายตาสั้นมาก' — high myopia = -6.00 D or more.
limitations: Consensus standard for research; other definitions quoted in the paper (e.g. for RAAB surveys) use ≤ −5.00 D for high myopia.

title: Incidence and progression of myopia in secondary school students: Follow-up for 2 years
key_findings: Prospective study of 363 secondary students aged 12-14 in Pathum Thani (82% coverage), examined yearly Sep 2015 - Mar 2017.
Within 19 months the cumulative proportion with myopia (SE ≤ -0.50 D) rose from 24.52% to 31.36%; myopia increased by -0.375 ± 0.247 D per year.
Myopia was not associated with sex (p=0.717) or age (p=0.791); authors state no previous Thai study had shown incidence and progression.
practical_applications: Only Thai figure we may quote, and only as 'การศึกษาหนึ่งในนักเรียนมัธยม จ.ปทุมธานี พบ ~1 ใน 4 มีสายตาผิดปกติ' — never generalise to 'เด็กไทย 25%'.
limitations: Single area, one school population; refraction mostly non-cycloplegic (auto + manifest; cycloplegia only in some cases).
Abstract only (journal page); the 24.52% is myopia in this group, not refractive error in Thai children generally.

title: Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults
authors: Singh S, Keller PR, Busija L, McMillan P, Makrai E, Lawrenson JG, Hull CC, Downie LE
key_findings: 17 RCTs, 619 adults; follow-up < 1 day to 5 weeks.
Visual fatigue: may be no difference vs non-blue-filtering lenses at < 1 week (low certainty).
Best-corrected visual acuity: probably little or no effect (moderate certainty, 1 trial, n=156).
Sleep: very uncertain (6 trials, mixed results). Macular health: no trial measured it.
practical_applications: Never claim blue-cut lenses reduce eye strain, improve sleep or protect the retina. Sell them, if at all, as a preference/comfort option with honest wording.
limitations: Short follow-up (< 1 day to 5 weeks); small trials; no meta-analysis possible; long-term outcomes unknown.

title: Are Blue Light-Blocking Glasses Worth It?
key_findings: 'There is no scientific evidence that the light coming from computer screens is damaging to the eyes'; the Academy does not recommend special eyewear for computer use or blue light-blocking glasses.

Eye strain comes from how people use their screens (decreased blinking), 'not by anything coming from the screens'; 'several studies suggest that blue light-blocking glasses do not improve symptoms of digital eye strain'.
Tips: sit about 25 inches (arm's length) from the screen, gaze slightly downward, 20-20-20 breaks, artificial tears when dry; avoid screens 2-3 hours before bed for sleep.
practical_applications: Cite AAO when replacing a blue-light claim with practical screen-habit advice.
limitations: Consumer page; AAO terms forbid copying content into AI programs, so only short paraphrase is kept here.

title: Digital eye strain: prevalence, measurement and amelioration
key_findings: DES (computer vision syndrome) prevalence 'may be 50% or more among computer users'; symptoms fall into accommodative/binocular-stress and external (dry eye) categories.
Cites a US survey of over 10,000 adults with 65% self-reported symptoms (females 69% vs males 60%).
Prevalence estimates vary widely between studies because definitions and questionnaires differ.
practical_applications: Frame screen discomfort as two mechanisms: focusing effort and dry surface (less blinking).
limitations: Narrative review; prevalence figures come from heterogeneous surveys.

title: The effects of breaks on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision: Testing the 20-20-20 rule
authors: Talens-Estarelles C, Cerviño A, García-Lázaro S, Fogelton A, Sheppard A, Wolffsohn JS
key_findings: 29 symptomatic computer users used webcam software giving personalised 20-20-20 reminders for 2 weeks.
DES and dry-eye symptoms decreased with reminders (p ≤ 0.045) but the improvement 'was not maintained one week after discontinuation'.
No binocular parameter changed except accommodative facility (p = 0.010); no ocular surface/tear film sign changed (p ≥ 0.089).
practical_applications: 20-20-20 may ease symptoms while practised; present as a habit that 'อาจช่วยให้สบายตาขึ้น'.
limitations: Small, uncontrolled before-after design, 2 weeks; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 35963776).

title: 20-20-20 Rule: Are These Numbers Justified?
key_findings: 30 young subjects did a 40-minute tablet reading task four times with 20-second breaks every 5, 10, 20 or 40 (no break) minutes.
Symptoms rose in all four trials (P < .001) but scheduled breaks had no significant effect on symptoms (P = .70), reading speed (P = .93) or accuracy (P = .55).

Conclusion: results 'do not support' 20-second scheduled breaks as a therapeutic intervention; the paper (quoted by Review of Optometry) adds this is not evidence that breaks in general are unhelpful.
practical_applications: Do not present 20-20-20 as proven; suggest real breaks and blinking.
limitations: Single 40-minute sessions in young adults; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 36473088) plus trade-press article.

title: TFOS DEWS II Definition and Classification Report
authors: Craig JP, Nichols KK, Akpek EK, Caffery B, Dua HS, Joo CK, Liu Z, Nelson JD, Nichols JJ, Tsubota K, Stapleton F
key_findings: Definition: dry eye is multifactorial, with loss of tear-film homeostasis as the central concept; tear film instability, hyperosmolarity, ocular surface inflammation and damage, and (for the first time) neurosensory abnormalities are included.

Classification: aqueous-deficient and evaporative dry eye exist as a continuum; diagnosis needs signs and symptoms, and the scheme allows signs without symptoms and symptoms without signs (e.g. neuropathic pain).
practical_applications: Dry eye is a disease to be diagnosed, not something glasses treat; shop content can mention blinking/breaks and refer persistent symptoms.
limitations: Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 28736335); prevalence figures are in a separate DEWS II report and were not read.

title: Defocus Incorporated Multiple Segments (DIMS) spectacle lenses slow myopia progression: a 2-year randomised clinical trial
authors: Lam CSY, Tang WC, Tse DYY, et al.
key_findings: 183 Hong Kong children aged 8-13, myopia -1.00 to -5.00 D; double-masked RCT DIMS vs single vision.
Progression -0.41 D vs -0.85 D (≈52% slower); axial elongation 0.21 vs 0.55 mm (≈62% less).
21.5% of DIMS wearers had no progression vs 7.4% single vision.
practical_applications: Allowed: 'เลนส์ชะลอสายตาสั้นบางชนิดมีงานวิจัย RCT ว่าชะลอการเพิ่มของสายตาสั้นในเด็กได้ราวครึ่งหนึ่งใน 2 ปี (ในเด็กจีนฮ่องกง)'. Never 'หยุด/รักษาสายตาสั้น'.
limitations: HOYA provided the lenses and spectacles and HOYA staff calculated/manufactured lenses; Chinese children only; 160 analysed (79 DIMS, 81 SV).

title: Spectacle Lenses With Aspherical Lenslets for Myopia Control vs Single-Vision Spectacle Lenses: A Randomized Clinical Trial
key_findings: Wenzhou, children 8-13, SER -0.75 to -4.75 D; HAL vs SAL vs single vision; 157 completed 2 years.
HAL vs SVL: progression -0.66 vs -1.46 D (0.80 D less, ~55%); axial 0.34 vs 0.69 mm (~51%).
Wearing ≥12 h/day: 67% (refraction) and 60% (axial length) slowing; dose-dependent on asphericity and wear time.
practical_applications: Myopia-control lenses only work when worn full-time — say this in any child-myopia content.
limitations: Essilor employed several authors, co-designed the study and analysis; single centre in China.

title: Spectacle Lenses With Highly Aspherical Lenslets for Myopia Control: A Randomized Clinical Trial
authors: Shen J, Hunt C, Young G, Drobe B
key_findings: Double-masked RCT at 9 US sites, children 6-12 years, SER -0.75 to -4.50 D; 159 randomised, 135 (84.9%) completed 24 months.
24-month myopia progression -0.25 D (HAL) vs -0.90 D (single vision): difference 0.64 D, 'a 71% relative reduction'; axial elongation 0.21 vs 0.45 mm, 'a 53% relative reduction'.
Adverse events 11.7% vs 14.6%, none serious or lens related; authors say the findings underlie FDA authorization of the device.
practical_applications: Suggests the effect is not limited to Chinese children — pending verification of the paper.
limitations: Industry trial (Drobe is an Essilor scientist); 2 years only; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 42623028).

title: Interventions for myopia control in children: a living systematic review and network meta-analysis
authors: Lawrenson JG, Shah R, Huntjens B, Downie LE, Virgili G, Dhakal R, Verkicharla PK, Li D, Mavi S, Kernohan A, Li T, Walline JJ
key_findings: 64 RCTs randomising 11,617 children aged 4-18 (60.9% of studies in China/Asia); 12-36 months; certainty very low to moderate. NMA networks poorly connected, so mostly direct pairwise estimates are reported.

At 1 year (control median SER change -0.65 D) SER progression may be reduced by high-dose atropine (MD 0.90 D), moderate-dose (0.65), low-dose atropine (0.38), peripheral-plus spectacles (0.51), multifocal soft contact lenses (0.26) and multifocal spectacles (0.14).
Undercorrected single-vision spectacles: little or no evidence they reduce progression (1 year MD −0.15 D, 95% CI −0.29 to 0.00; 2 years MD 0.02 D).

DIMS (Lam 2020) at 2 years: MD 0.55 D (95% CI 0.38 to 0.72) and axial −0.32 mm; 'inconclusive evidence on whether treatment cessation increases myopia progression'; no economic evaluations of myopia control found.
practical_applications: Position myopia-control lenses as 'หนึ่งในทางเลือกที่มีหลักฐาน' alongside atropine/ortho-K — decided with an eye professional.
limitations: 2023 version read (City, University of London repository copy); later living-review updates not read.

title: Effect of Time Spent Outdoors at School on the Development of Myopia Among Children in China: A Randomized Clinical Trial
authors: He M, Xiang F, Zeng Y, Mai J, Chen Q, Zhang J, Smith W, Rose K, Morgan IG
key_findings: Cluster RCT, grade 1 children in 12 Guangzhou primary schools, Oct 2010 - Oct 2013: 952 intervention, 951 control, mean age 6.6; one extra 40-minute outdoor class each school day plus encouragement of outdoor activity after school.
3-year cumulative myopia incidence 30.4% vs 39.5% (difference -9.1%, 95% CI -14.1% to -4.1%; P < .001).
SER change -1.42 vs -1.59 D (difference 0.17 D, P = .04); axial elongation 0.95 vs 0.98 mm, not significant (P = .07).
practical_applications: Allowed: 'การให้เด็กอยู่กลางแจ้งมากขึ้นช่วยลดโอกาสเริ่มสายตาสั้นได้บ้าง' — a modest, not total, effect.
limitations: Modest effect; China only; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 26372583); compliance figure not read.

title: Time spent in outdoor activities in relation to myopia prevention and control: a meta-analysis and systematic review
key_findings: 25 of 51 articles meta-analysed (23 in children).
Outdoor time protective for incident myopia: clinical trials RR 0.536 (95% CI 0.338-0.850); longitudinal cohorts RR 0.574 (0.395-0.834); cross-sectional OR 0.964.
Trials: myopic shift reduced by 0.30 D after 3 years; but among myopes only, no relationship between outdoor time and progression (R² = 0.00064).
practical_applications: Outdoor time = prevention-of-onset message, not a treatment for a child who already wears glasses.
limitations: Few trials; mix of designs; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 28251836).

title: Interventions to increase time spent outdoors for preventing incidence and progression of myopia in children
authors: Kido A, Miyake M, Watanabe N
key_findings: 5 RCTs (4 cluster-RCTs), 10,733 primary school children mostly in grades 1-2 (aged 6-9).
Incidence: 1 year 7.1% vs 9.5% (RR 0.82, 0.56-1.19, low certainty); 2 years 22.5% vs 26.7% (RR 0.84, 0.72-0.98, moderate certainty); 3 years 30.5% vs 39.8% (RR 0.77, 0.59-1.01, 1 study).

Refraction: MD 0.13 D less myopic shift at 2 years (moderate certainty); authors: interventions 'may potentially reduce the development of myopia' but low certainty makes conclusions on progression difficult. No adverse events reported.
practical_applications: Most conservative wording: 'อาจช่วยลดโอกาสเกิดสายตาสั้น'.
limitations: Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 38864362); applicability outside East Asia unclear.

title: Ultraviolet radiation (fact sheet)
key_findings: Acute: photokeratitis/photoconjunctivitis (painful, reversible).
Chronic: cataract, pterygium, cancers of/around the eye; possible role in AMD.
Of ~15 million cataract-blind people, 'some 10% may be due to exposure to UVR'.
Advises wraparound sunglasses blocking 99-100% UVA/UVB plus a broad-brimmed hat; water, sand and snow increase UV.
practical_applications: Basis for UV/beach scripts; supports wrap frames and hat advice.
limitations: Global estimate; 10% is an approximate attributable fraction.

title: Global Solar UV Index: A Practical Guide / WHO UV FAQ (ground reflection)
key_findings: 'Grass, soil or water reflect less than 10 per cent of incident UV radiation, sand reflects about 15 per cent, and sea foam about 25 per cent'; fresh snow 'almost doubles a person's UV exposure' (another section of the same page: snow up to 80%).
UV rises about 10% with every 1000 m altitude; light or thin clouds have little effect and may even increase UV; UVA is about 95% of UV reaching the surface.
practical_applications: Beach scripts: reflection is real but modest for water/sand; the bigger factor is time in strong overhead sun and peripheral light.
limitations: Archived WHO FAQ page (undated, Global Solar UV Index era).

title: A review of the epidemiologic evidence linking ultraviolet radiation and cataracts
key_findings: Reviewed against causality criteria; 'the majority of the 22 epidemiologic studies reviewed met most of the epidemiologic criteria for causality and support an association between UV-B and the development of cortical cataract and perhaps posterior subcapsular cataract'.
practical_applications: Say 'UV เป็นปัจจัยเสี่ยงหนึ่งของต้อกระจกบางชนิด' — age remains the main cause.
limitations: Observational evidence; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 12061276).

title: Assessment of the epidemiological evidence that exposure to solar ultraviolet radiation causes cataract
key_findings: Sufficient experimental evidence that artificial UV-B causes cortical opacities in laboratory animals; only limited evidence that solar UV-B causes cortical or posterior subcapsular cataract in humans.
Epidemiological evidence is consistent in suggesting nuclear cataract is not causally associated with solar UV-B.
practical_applications: Counterweight: never say 'แดดทำให้เป็นต้อกระจก' as a flat fact.
limitations: Old review; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 7635000; journal issue dated 1994).

title: Prevalence and risk factors of pterygium: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Rezvan F, Khabazkhoob M, Hooshmand E, Yekta A, Saatchi M, Hashemi H
key_findings: 68 articles, 415,911 participants, 24 countries: pooled pterygium prevalence 12% (95% CI 11-14%); 3% at age 10-20 rising to 19.5% over 80.
Odds ratios: sunlight exposure > 5 h 1.24 (1.11-1.36), rural residence 1.45, outdoor occupation 1.46, male 1.30, alcohol 1.17; sunglasses use 0.47 (0.19-0.57) and smoking 0.84 protective.
Prevalence range 0.07% (clinic-based, Saudi Arabia) to 53% (China).
practical_applications: 'ต้อเนื้อพบมากในคนที่อยู่กลางแจ้งนาน ๆ' is supported; the per-person risk increase is moderate.
limitations: Observational studies; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 29551597).

title: Occupational Exposure to Solar Radiation at Different Latitudes and Pterygium: A Systematic Review of the Last 10 Years of Scientific Literature
key_findings: Cites WHO: population attributable fraction of pterygium due to solar radiation 42-74%.

29 papers (2008-2017): pterygium prevalence rose with mean annual UV index (abstract wording: 'highly increased with latitude and mean annual UV index'); outdoor work, age and male sex are among the most relevant risk factors.
practical_applications: Hua Hin context: fishermen, beach vendors, outdoor workers — good real-life casting for UV stories (without naming real people).
limitations: Abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 29278403); the latitude wording is ambiguous in the abstract, so do not quote it.

title: Optical analysis and reappraisal of the peripheral light focusing theory of nasal pterygia formation
authors: King-Smith PE, Mauger TF, Begley CG, Tankam P
key_findings: Pterygia are far more often nasal (one cited series: 93.6% nasal, 15.5 times more common than temporal); Coroneo's peripheral light focusing (PLF) theory says oblique UV through the temporal cornea is concentrated onto the nasal limbus.

Re-analysis at fixed limbal positions: 'the limbal UV irradiation of the nasal limbus from the PLF was not sufficient to explain the strong nasal location preference'; other explanations such as temporal-to-nasal tear flow should be considered.
practical_applications: Wrap/side coverage advice is reasonable (WHO/AAO also advise wraparound), but don't present 'แสงจากด้านข้างถูกโฟกัส 20 เท่า' as settled.
limitations: Optical modelling study; contested area.

title: How to Choose the Best Sunglasses to Avoid Sun Damage; The Sun, UV Light and Your Eyes (AAO consumer pages)
key_findings: Look for '100% UV protection' or 'UV absorption up to 400nm' (UV400); 'don't be fooled into thinking the darker the lens, the more they'll protect your eyes'.
'Polarization itself does not provide UV protection'; coloured or mirror lenses do not add UV protection; expensive does not mean safer.
Clouds don't block UV; oversize and wraparound frames reduce side entry; wear a broad-brimmed hat; UV is stronger when reflected off water, ice or snow.
practical_applications: Polarised = glare, UV400 = UV — two separate features; good explainer carousel.
limitations: Consumer pages ('How to Choose the Best Sunglasses', 'The Sun, UV Light and Your Eyes'); the news-release URL itself rendered no text. AAO terms forbid copying into AI programs, so paraphrase only.

title: ISO 12312-1:2022 Eye and face protection — Sunglasses and related eyewear — Part 1: Sunglasses for general use
key_findings: ISO catalogue page confirms the 2022 edition: applies to afocal (plano) sunglasses and clip-ons for general use, including road use and driving; excludes sunglasses medically prescribed for attenuating solar radiation, eclipse viewers (ISO 12312-2) and occupational/sport protectors.
Filter categories and the driving rule are known here only through the College of Optometrists' summary of the 2013 edition (see CollegeOptomTints).
practical_applications: Category 4 (very dark) lenses: never advertise as driving sunglasses.
limitations: Standard text not read (paywalled; ISO forbids using its content with AI tools beyond public pages).

title: Tints and driving (clinical guidance)
key_findings: Per BS EN ISO 12312-1:2013: category 0 >80-100% luminous transmittance, 1 >43-80%, 2 >18-43%, 3 >8-18%, 4 >3-8%.

Filters suitable for road use and driving must be category 0-3 (so not category 4), with spectral transmittance ≥ 0.2 × Tv at 475-650 nm and signal-light Q ≥ 0.8 for red and yellow, ≥ 0.6 for yellow, green and blue.
'Sunglass filters with a luminous transmittance of less than 75% are not suitable for road use in twilight or at night.'
practical_applications: Use when making 'เลือกความเข้มเลนส์กันแดด' content.
limitations: UK guidance quoting the 2013 edition of the standard.

title: Methods for Estimating Lens Thickness
key_findings: Sag s ≈ (d/2)² · F / (2000 (n − 1)) with d in mm, F in dioptres: sag rises with power and with the square of diameter, falls as index rises.
Minus lens: edge = s2 − s1 + centre thickness; plus lens: centre = s1 − s2 + edge thickness.
Minimum centre thickness for minus lenses typically 1.0-2.2 mm depending on material and design; rimless/safety may be thicker.
practical_applications: Explain why a smaller, well-centred frame thins a minus lens as much as a higher index does (see README table).
limitations: Thin-lens approximation; manufacturer-era trade article; modern aspheric designs change real numbers.

title: Lens Material Properties (EyeWiki)
authors: Oke I, Sanjiv N, Aggarwal S, Reddy V (AAO EyeWiki)
key_findings: High-index: ≥ 1.60, generally lower Abbe value; lower Abbe → more chromatic aberration (colour fringing in periphery, stronger Rx).
Polycarbonate: superior impact resistance, strong UV absorption, low Abbe; Trivex: high Abbe, light, high impact; CR-39: lower index, blocks ~80% UV untreated.
Reviewed 5 Aug 2026.
practical_applications: 'บางสุด' is not always 'ดีที่สุด' — index trades against Abbe value.
limitations: Few exact numbers on the page.

title: ZEISS finished single vision lens fact sheets (material index, Abbe)
key_findings: 1.59 polycarbonate listed with Abbe 32 (other sources 30-32).
1.74 listed with Abbe vd 32.6 / ve 32 (other trade tables ~33).
practical_applications: Reference numbers for lens-material carousel: 1.50 ≈ 58, 1.56 ≈ 36-43 (varies by maker), 1.60 ≈ 40-42, 1.67 ≈ 31-32, 1.74 ≈ 32-33 — check the exact product sheet before posting.
limitations: Values for 1.50/1.56/1.60/1.67 not read from the sheet this session (2023 PDF 404); figures in the application line are typical trade values to verify.
Re-checked 2026-11-25: URL returns 404 or renders no text to automated fetch; findings stay search-summary only and must not carry a claim on their own.

title: Transitions XTRActive New Generation (product page)
authors: Nikon Lenswear (Transitions licensee); Shamir Thailand page
key_findings: Manufacturer claim: XTRActive New Generation is 'the only photochromic lens achieving category 2 levels' behind the windshield: 18%-43% transmittance at 23 °C (polycarbonate and 1.5 grey).
Claims category 3 (<18% T) outdoors at 35 °C and 100% UVA/UVB blocking; 'photochromic performance is influenced by temperature, UV exposure and lens material'.
practical_applications: Never sell standard photochromic as 'ใส่ขับรถแทนแว่นกันแดดได้'.
limitations: Manufacturer test conditions; the polarised version was not checked on this page.

title: Self-tinting lenses for more comfortable vision, flexibility and protection (ZEISS)
key_findings: ZEISS: 'a huge amount of UV rays are absorbed by a car's windshield, which has an effect on the lens performance'; PhotoFusion X retains more tint in the car than earlier generations, but 'sunglasses are still recommended for longer trips'.
'Self-tinting lenses darken less in bright sunlight when outdoor temperatures are high', so ZEISS recommends carrying sunglasses in warmer areas.
Darkens in 15-30 seconds and clears in as little as 2 minutes (manufacturer figures).
practical_applications: Hua Hin is hot: tell customers photochromic may not get as dark at the beach at noon as in brochures.
limitations: Manufacturer page; no quantified temperature curve; patent and retailer guides not re-read.

title: Troubleshooting varifocals (CPD article)
key_findings: 'Adaption periods of around two to four weeks should be emphasised to first-time wearers'; expectations (e.g. a narrower reading zone) should be managed at the dispense.
Common remake causes: fitting heights measured off eye level or with slouched posture; check prescription, fitting cross and lens design (trial frame) before blaming the lens.
Manufacturers typically assume a pantoscopic angle of around 8-10° for conventional PALs; more tilt brings the near zone closer and widens the near field.
practical_applications: Progressive content must mention adaptation and correct fitting; no 'ใส่ปุ๊บชัดปั๊บทุกคน'.
limitations: Practitioner CPD article with case examples; gives no non-tolerance rate.

title: The impact of different lenses on visual and musculoskeletal complaints in VDU workers with work-related neck complaints: a randomized controlled trial
key_findings: RCT: 35 VDU workers aged 45-65 from a financial holding in Ghent with neck complaints, VDU progressive (n=18) vs general progressive (n=17).
Both groups improved in visual fatigue and neck pain at 3 and 6 months; 'little difference in effect of the different lenses'; the VDU group rated its lenses more suitable for VDU work.
Cites Horgen et al.: a 1-year RCT of 3 VDU progressive designs vs single vision found a significant neck-pain reduction with one VDU lens type.
practical_applications: Office lenses: present as comfort for long desk work with a wider intermediate zone, not as a neck-pain treatment.
limitations: Small; neck-pain change below the minimal clinically important difference.

title: Guidelines for Appropriate Referral of Persons with Possible Eye Diseases or Injury
key_findings: Prompt referral to an ophthalmologist for: failure to achieve normal acuity; significant eye injury, eye pain or periocular trauma; flashes, recent floaters, halos, transient dimming or distortion, obscured vision, loss of vision, pain in eye/lids/orbit, double vision, excessive tearing.

Also: any visual field loss, media opacities or fundus/optic nerve abnormalities, lid/orbit tumour or swelling or protruding eye, inflammation with or without discharge, strabismus not corrected by glasses, abnormal IOP or glaucoma family history, diabetes without a recent retinal exam, thyroid eye signs.
practical_applications: Red-flag list in FACT_CHECK_WORKFLOW and in any shop post about 'when to see a doctor'.
limitations: US professional guidance (2014 PDF).

title: ZEISS Individual 2 fitting & dispensing guide; ZEISS Individual SV white paper
key_findings: Default pantoscopic tilt 9° and vertex distance 12.5 mm if not measured; fitting height range 13-35 mm; monocular PD measured with pupillometer.
Individual lenses are optimised to measured tilt, wrap and vertex.
ZEISS webinar: 2 mm centration error can reduce binocular field of view by up to 25% (manufacturer claim).
practical_applications: Shop-craft content: 'วัดค่าเฉพาะตัว' (PD, fitting height, tilt) as a real reason a progressive works or fails.
limitations: Older guides (2010-2020); manufacturer figures.
Re-checked 2026-11-25: URL returns 404 or renders no text to automated fetch; findings stay search-summary only and must not carry a claim on their own.

title: How to Choose the Glasses Frame Material That's Right for You (AAO)
key_findings: Titanium frames: 'very strong, lightweight and corrosion-resistant' and hypoallergenic; Flexon is a titanium alloy, also hypoallergenic.
Monel (mixed metals) 'may have nickel or other metals that can cause allergic reactions', though most have a protective coating; stainless steel is light, strong, corrosion-resistant and cheaper.

Plastics: zyl (cellulose acetate) easy for opticians to adjust; blended nylon strong and light for sport/wraparound; Optyl becomes malleable when heated; plastic frames break more easily than metal and colour may fade.
practical_applications: Hot car dashboard in Hua Hin can deform acetate — useful care tip.
limitations: AAO consumer page only; the All About Vision page was not reachable, so claims about TR90 and nickel in stainless steel are not verified.

title: Ministry drafts regulation on eyesight-testing and spectacle-fitting businesses
key_findings: 17 Jun 2026: MOPH draft ministerial regulation would make 'กิจการตรวจวัดสายตาประกอบแว่น' a health-business establishment (Health Establishment law).
Shops need a licence; testers must register and complete a specific training course.
Scope: refractive errors (myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia) in people aged 12+; no eye-muscle exams; under-12s and eye-muscle problems go to a medical facility/specialist.
Effective 180 days after Gazette publication; existing shops get 180 days to apply. Status: draft (public hearing).
practical_applications: Do not market 'ตรวจสายตาเด็ก' at the shop for under-12s if this rule is enacted; refer to an eye doctor.
limitations: News report of a draft; check Royal Gazette for final text. Confirmed by Thansettakij (17 Jun 2026).

title: Optometry Association complains of delayed professional legislation
key_findings: 18 Jun 2026: Optometry Association of Thailand asked the House health committee to speed up optometry legislation; slow licence renewals; unlicensed people impersonating optometrists.

No optometry council (สภา) is mentioned; Thai news (Khaosod/Matichon snippets) says optometry is a branch of the Art of Healing (พ.ร.บ.การประกอบโรคศิลปะ พ.ศ. 2542) and a draft Royal Decree on optometry was open for comment until 13 Nov 2026.
practical_applications: Only call staff 'นักทัศนมาตร' if they hold the licence; otherwise 'ช่างวัดสายตา/ผู้ตรวจวัดสายตา'. Do not refer to 'สภาการทัศนมาตรศาสตร์' as an existing regulator.
limitations: News; the Art of Healing / Royal Decree detail is from search snippets only.

title: Thai FDA issues medical device advertising regulations
key_findings: Thai FDA announcement B.E. 2568 (2025) on medical device advertising, effective 4 Jan 2025, revokes the B.E. 2564 (2021) announcement; anyone advertising a medical device needs an FDA licence (Form Kor Por. 2), valid up to 3 years.

Prohibited: false or exaggerated benefits, quality, standards, components or source (Section 59(1), Medical Device Act B.E. 2551) and Schedule 1 words such as 'best, excellent, special, miraculous, perfect, completely cured, instantaneous, the safest, No.1, definitely, superior, no side effects'; also endorsement by individuals and comparison with other operators' devices.
Ads must show the advertiser, the ad licence number and warnings; devices exempted by MOPH announcement are outside this rule.
practical_applications: Treat lens-benefit claims (myopia control, blue light) as medical-device claims: no exaggeration, use only manufacturer-approved wording, consider whether Thai FDA ad approval applies (contact lenses clearly do).
limitations: Consultancy summary, not the Gazette text; whether spectacle lenses/frames are exempt was NOT confirmed.

title: Varilux XR series wins the Silmo d'Or (EssilorLuxottica newsroom)
key_findings: Claims 9/10 wearers experienced 'instant sharpness' at all distances and in motion; 95% adapted by day one.
Basis: Eurosyn in-life study, France 2022, n=73 progressive wearers, 2 weeks, sponsored by Essilor.
practical_applications: If quoted: 'จากการทดสอบของผู้ผลิตกับผู้ใช้ 73 คน' — never as independent fact.
limitations: Sponsor study, small n, no independent replication found.
Re-checked 2026-11-25: URL returns 404 or renders no text to automated fetch; findings stay search-summary only and must not carry a claim on their own.

title: In conversation with Dr Natalia Vlasak about the Miyosmart iQ spectacle lens (AOP Optometry Today)
authors: HOYA Vision Care; AOP Optometry Today
key_findings: HOYA (interview): Miyosmart iQ 12-month RCT in children aged 4-12 showed 'no myopia progression on average' and, per ARVO 2026 results, halted 'clinically relevant myopia progression' in nine out of 10 children.
Previous-generation MiYOSMART slowed progression 'on average by 59% at the 24-month wearing period'; iQ changes: segments closer to centre, segment power +3.5 D to +4.5 D, wider treatment zone.
practical_applications: Use the peer-reviewed Lam 2020 numbers, not '>100%' marketing figures.
limitations: Company statements; iQ data conference-only, not peer-reviewed; the earlier '>100% efficacy' wording and a US approval disclaimer were not on the page read.

title: ZEISS BlueGuard (product page, fact sheet)
key_findings: Claims BlueGuard blocks 'up to 40% of potentially harmful blue light' (BVB metric) with full UV protection, built into the lens material.
'Up to 50% fewer reflections of digital blue light' than ZEISS's own DuraVision Plus BlueProtect coating.
'93% of wearers feel less digital eye strain' and 95% prefer BlueGuard; basis: consumer acceptance survey, n=187 wearers in China, May 2021.
practical_applications: Allowed: 'ลดแสงสีฟ้าบางส่วน สะท้อนน้อยลง (ข้อมูลผู้ผลิต)'. Not allowed: 'ลดอาการตาล้า/ป้องกันจอประสาทตาเสื่อม'.
limitations: Manufacturer page; it says blue-light lenses alleviate DES, which Singh 2023 Cochrane and AAO do not support.

title: Presbyopia (NEI eye conditions page)
key_findings: Presbyopia makes near vision hard for middle-aged and older adults; 'Everyone gets presbyopia as they get older — usually after age 45.'
Cause: with age the lens gets harder and less flexible and stops focusing light correctly; 'Many people have another refractive error in addition to presbyopia.'
It gets worse over time but 'usually stops getting worse after age 65'; managed with reading glasses, prescribed lenses or contact lenses.
practical_applications: Supports 'ทุกคนเป็นได้ แม้เคยสายตาดีหรือสายตาสั้น' and onset 'ราววัย 40 กลาง ๆ ขึ้นไป' (NEI says usually after 45).
limitations: Consumer page; replaces StatPearls (NCBI blocked by a browser check).

title: Analysis of pterygium size and induced corneal astigmatism
key_findings: 77 eyes with unilateral primary pterygium: corneal astigmatism 1.2 ± 0.9 D vs 0.6 ± 0.5 D in fellow eyes (P < 0.0001); with-the-rule 49.4%, against-the-rule 36.4%, oblique 14.3%.
Extension correlated best with astigmatism (r = 0.462), then total area (r = 0.447) and width (r = 0.348).
'Pterygium induced 2 D of corneal astigmatism when its extension exceeded 2.2 mm, width exceeded 5 mm, or total area exceeded 6.25 mm²'.
practical_applications: Supports 'ต้อเนื้อที่ลามเข้ากระจกตาทำให้สายตาเอียงได้'; refer to an eye doctor, do not imply glasses fix it.
limitations: Single-centre, 77 eyes; abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 18434847). Replaces 'Kampitak2003Astig': that title actually belongs to this paper and the figures recorded for Kampitak (243 eyes, 2.25 mm) could not be found.
